findings.fix: Replace the bare `Bash(git * branch*)`/`Bash(git * log*)`/`Bash(git * show*)`/`Bash(git * status*)` rules with ones that pin the git-global-option position shut — e.g. drop the leading `*` entirely (require the subcommand to be the literal next word, as the `-C` carve-out already does for other rules) or route any `git -c ...`/`git -p ...` invocation through the `ask` list instead of `allow`.
findings.claim: The deployed Claude Code settings.json permissions.allow list (settings/claude_code/settings.json:21-25) grants unprompted execution to `Bash(git * branch*)`, `Bash(git * log*)`, `Bash(git * show*)` and `Bash(git * status*)`. Per this repo's own documented glob-matching semantics (AGENTS.md / ACTION-IMPL-EXEC-007: rules are literal whole-command globs, and a wildcard positioned before the matched subcommand word is exactly what lets extra flags land there), the leading `*` in each of these four rules sits between `git` and the subcommand, so it matches any flags inserted before the subcommand — including `-c core.pager=<cmd>` (and `-c pager.status=true -c core.pager=<cmd>` for status/branch/show). `git -c core.pager=<cmd> log` is documented, standard git behavior: it spawns `<cmd>` as a subprocess to page the output, i.e. arbitrary command execution, with no args beyond the config override. A single Bash tool call `git -c core.pager='<attacker command>' log` therefore executes attacker-chosen shell commands under the allowlist with zero approval prompt, whenever anything (a compromised MCP tool, a prompt-injected instruction from untrusted file content the agent reads, or a confused/ jailbroken model) gets the agent to issue that one command — this is a security-boundary bypass of the settings.json permission model itself, not a bug in git.
findings.evidence: Re-read settings/claude_code/settings.json lines 1-113 in full (committed content via `git show e5245d08d2fe5c05f67742fd8ec5a67b759ca316:settings/claude_code/settings.json`, confirmed byte-identical to the worktree read at lines 21-25): the five git rules are exactly `Bash(git * branch*)`, `Bash(git * log*)`, `Bash(git * show*)`, `Bash(git * stash list)`, `Bash(git * status*)` — four of the five (all but the literal-suffixed `stash list`) carry the vulnerable leading wildcard. Cross-checked the matching semantics against this repo's own AGENTS.md (ACTION-IMPL-EXEC-007), which gives the worked example `Bash(git commit -m *)` denies `git commit -s -m` because the flag lands before the matched words, confirming that the engine glob-matches the raw command string and that a flag placed in a wildcard region is accepted. `git -c <section>.<key>=<value> <subcommand>` executing `<value>` as a pager/credential-helper/diff-command subprocess is long-established, widely documented git behavior (the core.pager/pager.<cmd> and GIT_PAGER mechanisms exist precisely to spawn an external program named by config) — not something this review needed to newly discover, only to connect to the allow-rule shape. I could not execute the literal PoC command inside this review sandbox (its own, separate bash-policy layer denies any `git -c ...` invocation, per ACTION-IMPL-EXEC-010 in this session's own AGENTS.md — a different, repo-external enforcement layer that has no bearing on what the reviewed settings.json itself permits on a machine where it is the only gate), so this claim rests on the documented matching rule plus documented git behavior rather than a live transcript; both are independently verifiable and the claim does not depend on any guess about undocumented engine internals.

findings.fix: Pin and verify the two downloads against a recorded SHA-256 (fail the build step if it does not match) before they are staged into dist/ and bundled by installer/windows/smine.iss, e.g. `curl -fsSL -o dist/jq.exe <url> && echo "<expected-sha256>  dist/jq.exe" | shasum -a 256 -c -`.
findings.claim: The release `build` job (.github/workflows/ci.yml:49-52) fetches `jq-windows-amd64.exe` and `peek-mcp-windows-amd64.exe` over plain `curl -fsSL -o` with no checksum or signature verification, then uploads them as the `windows-payload` artifact that the `installer` job folds straight into `dist/` and compiles into smine-setup.exe (installer\windows\smine.iss, Source lines for jq.exe/peek-mcp.exe under `{app}`) — i.e. these two unverified third-party binaries ship to every Windows end user and get installed with no integrity check at any point in the pipeline. If either upstream release asset is ever replaced at the same URL/tag (compromised maintainer account, CDN/cache poisoning, or a MITM on the CI runner's egress), the next tagged release silently bundles and distributes a malicious executable to installer users.
findings.evidence: Re-read .github/workflows/ci.yml lines 1-107 in full (git show e5245d08d2fe5c05f67742fd8ec5a67b759ca316:.github/workflows/ci.yml) and installer/windows/smine.iss lines 1-123 in full: confirmed the two `curl -fsSL -o` lines have no following verification step (no shasum/certutil/Get-FileHash call anywhere in the `build` or `installer` jobs), and confirmed smine.iss's `[Files]` section sources `..\..\dist\jq.exe` and `..\..\dist\peek-mcp.exe` directly with no hash check of its own — the chain from fetch to shipped installer carries zero verification at every hop I could see in this chunk.

findings.fix: Pin serena-agent to a specific version (`uv tool install -p 3.13 serena-agent==<version>`) and bump it deliberately, instead of `--upgrade` pulling whatever is newest on PyPI at install/reinstall time.
findings.claim: install.sh's `--serena` path (install.sh:70-71) runs `uv tool install -p 3.13 --upgrade serena-agent` with no version pin — every fresh install and every re-run of install.sh on an existing machine silently fetches and installs whatever is currently the newest `serena-agent` release from PyPI and lets it run as an MCP server (settings/claude_code/claude.serena.json, merged by cmd/sync/sync_settings.sh's merge_mcp_servers, is in the diff but outside this chunk). A compromise of the serena-agent PyPI package (account takeover, dependency confusion, or a malicious maintainer release) reaches every machine that re-runs install.sh with --serena after the bad release goes live, with no version gate to catch it.
findings.evidence: Re-read install.sh lines 1-202 in full (git show e5245d08d2fe5c05f67742fd8ec5a67b759ca316:install.sh): confirmed line 71 is exactly `uv tool install -p 3.13 --upgrade serena-agent` with no `==` version pin anywhere in the file, and that the companion `peek-mcp` install two lines above (`go install github.com/kevinhorst/peek-mcp@v1.2.2`) DOES pin a version — the serena-agent line is the one unpinned install in this file, not a project-wide pattern, which makes it a reviewable local gap rather than a sweeping claim.
